q: A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the superposition of two waves of the same type having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in _____ directions.
e: A stationary wave needs two waves of the same type, equal amplitude and speed, travelling opposite ways. A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the superposition of two waves of the same type having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in opposite directions. The same or perpendicular is not this quantity.

q: Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not spread out but remain in the region in which they are produced, so they are also called _____ waves.
e: A stationary wave stays in one region, so it is also called a standing wave. Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not spread out but remain in the region in which they are produced, so they are also called standing waves. Do not trade standing for traveling or transverse.

q: When two or more waves pass the same point, the resultant wave at that point is the sum of the individual waves. This is called the principle of _____
e: Superposition: the resultant at a point is the sum of the individual displacements. When two or more waves pass the same point, the resultant wave at that point is the sum of the individual waves. This is called the principle of superposition. Interference or reflection is not this quantity.

q: In a stationary wave, the points that are always stationary are called _____
e: Nodes never move. They sit half a wavelength apart. In a stationary wave, the points that are always stationary are called nodes. Antinodes or crests is not this quantity.

q: In a stationary wave, the points between nodes that vibrate with the largest amplitude are called _____
e: Antinodes are the peaks of vibration, midway between nodes. In a stationary wave, the points between nodes that vibrate with the largest amplitude are called antinodes. Do not trade antinodes for nodes or troughs.

q: The distance between two successive nodes (or) antinodes in a stationary wave is equal to _____
e: Antinodes are the peaks of vibration, midway between nodes. The distance between two successive nodes (or) antinodes in a stationary wave is equal to (λ)/(2). λ or (λ)/(4) is a different relation from (λ)/(2).

q: The distance from a node to the nearest antinode in a stationary wave is equal to _____
e: From a node to the next antinode is λ/4. The distance from a node to the nearest antinode in a stationary wave is equal to (λ)/(4). (λ)/(2) or λ is a different relation from (λ)/(4).

q: If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be _____ interference.
e: Interference needs coherent waves. Bright fringes are constructive; dark fringes are destructive. If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be constructive interference. Do not trade constructive for destructive or neutral.

q: If the resultant wave has zero amplitude, this is said to be _____ interference.
e: Interference needs coherent waves. Bright fringes are constructive; dark fringes are destructive. If the resultant wave has zero amplitude, this is said to be destructive interference. Constructive or partial is not this quantity.

q: Sound waves which travel in air when we speak are examples of _____ waves.
e: Speech in air is a progressive wave, not a standing wave. Sound waves which travel in air when we speak are examples of progressive waves. Stationary or longitudinal only is not this quantity.

q: In musical instruments such as violin and mandolin, the stretched strings produce _____ waves.
e: A string fixed at both ends has nodes at the ends. The fundamental wavelength is 2L. In musical instruments such as violin and mandolin, the stretched strings produce stationary waves. Do not trade stationary for progressive or electromagnetic.

q: For a string of length $l$ rigidly fixed at both ends, the wavelength of the $n^{\text{th}}$ harmonic is given by $\lambda_n =$ _____
e: For a string of length l rigidly fixed at both ends, the wavelength of the n^th harmonic is given by λ_n = (2l)/(n). (l)/(n) or (4l)/(n) is a different relation from (2l)/(n).

q: The frequencies of a vibrating string of length $l$ are given by $f_n =$ _____
e: The frequencies of a vibrating string of length l are given by f_n = (nv)/(2l). (nv)/(4l) or (v)/(nl) is a different relation from (nv)/(2l).

q: Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or the _____ harmonic.
e: The fundamental is the lowest standing-wave frequency. Higher ones are harmonics or overtones. Vibration of a string in one single segment is called the fundamental or the first harmonic. Second or third is not this quantity.

q: A musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note is called a(n) _____
e: The fundamental is the lowest standing-wave frequency. Higher ones are harmonics or overtones. A musical tone which is part of the harmonic series above a fundamental note is called a(n) overtone. Undertone or resonance is not this quantity.

q: The velocity $v$ of a wave in a vibrating string depends on tension $T$ and mass per unit length $\mu$ as $v =$ _____
e: The velocity v of a wave in a vibrating string depends on tension T and mass per unit length μ as v = √((T)/(μ)). (T)/(μ) or √(Tμ) is a different relation from √((T)/(μ)).

q: Mass per unit length $\mu$ of a string is the ratio of its mass to its _____
e: Mass per unit length μ of a string is the ratio of its mass to its length. Do not trade length for volume or density.

q: If $A$ is the uniform cross-sectional area and $\rho$ is the density of the string material, then mass per unit length $\mu =$ _____
e: Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. If A is the uniform cross-sectional area and ρ is the density of the string material, then mass per unit length μ = ρ A. (ρ)/(A) or (A)/(ρ) is a different relation from ρ A. Ρ a is what this sentence is naming. Stay with the quantity named in this sentence.

q: For a vibrating string fixed at both ends, only certain specific _____ can occur.
e: For a vibrating string fixed at both ends, only certain specific frequencies can occur. Amplitudes or velocities is not this quantity.

q: The second harmonic of a vibrating string is also known as the _____ overtone.
e: Harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency. The second harmonic of a vibrating string is also known as the first overtone. Second or fundamental is not this quantity.

q: Resonance occurs when the frequency of the driving force equals the _____ of the system.
e: Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period. Resonance occurs when the frequency of the driving force equals the natural frequency of the system. Do not trade natural frequency for resonant frequency or damped frequency.

q: Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to oscillate in the absence of any _____
e: Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period. Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system tends to oscillate in the absence of any driving force. Do not trade driving force for friction or mass.

q: In a resonance column experiment, a node is formed at the _____ end of the tube.
e: Standing waves stay put with nodes and antinodes. Progressive waves travel and carry energy. In a resonance column experiment, a node is formed at the closed end of the tube. Open or middle is not this quantity.

q: In a resonance column experiment, an antinode is formed at the _____ end of the tube.
e: Standing waves stay put with nodes and antinodes. Progressive waves travel and carry energy. In a resonance column experiment, an antinode is formed at the open end of the tube. Closed or center is not this quantity.

q: For a closed organ pipe, the wavelength of the $n^{\text{th}}$ harmonic is $\lambda_n =$ _____, where $n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$
e: For a closed organ pipe, the wavelength of the n^th harmonic is λ_n = (4l)/(n), where n = 1, 3, 5, dots. (2l)/(n) or (l)/(n) is a different relation from (4l)/(n).

q: The resonant frequency of a closed organ pipe is $f_n =$ _____, where $n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$
e: Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period. The resonant frequency of a closed organ pipe is f_n = (nv)/(4l), where n = 1, 3, 5, dots. (nv)/(2l) or (v)/(4nl) is a different relation from (nv)/(4l).

q: A closed organ pipe produces only _____ harmonics.
e: Harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency. A closed organ pipe produces only odd harmonics. Do not trade odd for even or all.

q: In an open organ pipe, the wavelength of the $n^{\text{th}}$ harmonic is $\lambda_n =$ _____
e: In an open organ pipe, the wavelength of the n^th harmonic is λ_n = (2l)/(n). (4l)/(n) or (l)/(2n) is a different relation from (2l)/(n).

q: The frequencies of a vibrating air column in an open organ pipe are $f_n =$ _____
e: The frequencies of a vibrating air column in an open organ pipe are f_n = (nv)/(2l). (nv)/(4l) or (v)/(2nl) is a different relation from (nv)/(2l).

q: A flute can be modeled as a pipe that is _____
e: A flute can be modeled as a pipe that is open at both ends. Closed at one end or closed at both ends is not this quantity.

q: A clarinet can be modeled as a pipe that is _____
e: A clarinet can be modeled as a pipe that is closed at one end. Open at both ends or closed at both ends is not this quantity.

q: Beats are the periodic fluctuation heard in the intensity of sound when two sound waves of slightly different _____ interfere.
e: Lenses refract. Light is an electromagnetic wave and also a particle. Beats are the periodic fluctuation heard in the intensity of sound when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies interfere. Amplitudes or wavelengths is not this quantity.

q: The beat frequency is given by $f =$ _____
e: Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period. The beat frequency is given by f = |f_1 - f_2|. f_1 + f_2 or (f_1 + f_2)/(2) is a different relation from |f_1 - f_2|.

q: If two tuning forks of 512 Hz and 516 Hz vibrate simultaneously, the beat frequency is _____
e: Frequency is the number of turns per second, the reciprocal of the period. If two tuning forks of 512 Hz and 516 Hz vibrate simultaneously, the beat frequency is 4 Hz. Do not trade 4 Hz for 1028 Hz or 2 Hz.

q: The intensity of a wave is the power (or energy per unit time) transported per unit _____
e: Work is F · s. Power is work per second, in watts. The intensity of a wave is the power (or energy per unit time) transported per unit cross-sectional area. Volume or length is not this quantity.

q: In SI units, the unit of intensity of a wave is _____
e: In SI units, the unit of intensity of a wave is watt per metre squared (W m^-2). Do not trade watt per metre squared (W m^-2) for joule per second or newton per metre.

q: For a point source, sound intensity at distance $r$ is given by $I =$ _____
e: For a point source, sound intensity at distance r is given by I = (P)/(4π r²). (P)/(2π r) or (P)/(r) is a different relation from (P)/(4π r²).

q: Intensity of a wave varies inversely with the square of the distance from the source. This is known as the _____ law.
e: Intensity of a wave varies inversely with the square of the distance from the source. This is known as the inverse square law. Do not trade inverse square for direct square or logarithmic.

q: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the square of the _____ of the wave.
e: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude of the wave. Do not trade amplitude for frequency or wavelength.

q: Sound levels of 140 to 150 dB can _____
a: rupture eardrums and cause permanent hearing loss
have no effect on human ears
e: Sound levels of 140 to 150 dB can rupture eardrums and cause permanent hearing loss. Do not trade rupture eardrums and cause permanent hearing loss for improve hearing temporarily or have no effect on human ears.
